"""S mechanism: logic variables and a suspension queue.

Owns: Var, deref() (the variables of the S mechanisms; propagate.py accepts
them as its variables, search.py has none). Uses search.py's trail
convention (a list of undo callables) when a trail is given.

A Var is unbound until it is bound once. Binding a Var to another unbound Var
makes them one variable; binding to anything else gives it that value.
deref(t) follows bindings to an unbound Var or a value. Values are compared
with ==; terms are not unified inside (a value that contains Vars is just a
value).

Queue holds goals (zero-argument callables) waiting on unknowns:
  wait(goal, *vars) -- goal is held until any one of vars is bound to a value
                       (if one already is, or none is given, it is ready now);
                       a goal waiting on several vars is woken once;
  bind(v, x, trail) -- bind v to x and wake the goals waiting on v; True if
                       consistent, False if both are values and differ
                       (nothing is changed then);
  run()             -- run ready goals until none is ready; returns how many ran.
Order (fairness): ready goals run first in, first out. A binding appends the
goals it wakes at the back of the ready queue, in the order they suspended.
So a goal, once woken, runs after every goal ready before it and before every
goal woken after it: none waits for ever while each goal returns. A goal may
wait again (to wait for all of several variables, wait on the next unbound
one) and may bind, which wakes others behind it. Binding two unbound Vars
together wakes nothing: the goals of the first wait on the merged variable.

`held` (key -> goal; keys increase in suspension order) is the suspended goals, `ready` the
goals woken and not yet run; a caller may register either. With a trail, a
binding is undone by search.undo: the variable is unbound again and the goals
it woke are held again. Undo only with the ready queue empty (call run()
first): a goal that has run is not un-run, though its trailed bindings are
undone.
"""


class Var:
    __slots__ = ("ref", "waiting", "name")

    def __init__(self, name="_"):
        self.ref = self     # itself while unbound
        self.waiting = []   # keys of goals in Queue.held
        self.name = name

    def __repr__(self):
        t = deref(self)
        return t.name if isinstance(t, Var) else repr(t)


def deref(t):
    while isinstance(t, Var) and t.ref is not t:
        t = t.ref
    return t


class Queue:
    def __init__(self):
        self.held = {}
        self.ready = []
        self.key = 0

    def wait(self, goal, *vars):
        vs = [deref(v) for v in vars]
        if not vs or not all(isinstance(v, Var) for v in vs):
            self.ready.append(goal)
            return
        self.key += 1
        self.held[self.key] = goal
        for v in vs:
            v.waiting.append(self.key)

    def bind(self, v, x, trail=None):
        a, b = deref(v), deref(x)
        if a is b:
            return True
        if not isinstance(a, Var):
            a, b = b, a
        if not isinstance(a, Var):
            return a == b
        a.ref = b
        if isinstance(b, Var):
            n = len(b.waiting)
            b.waiting += a.waiting

            def back():
                a.ref = a
                del b.waiting[n:]
        else:
            woken = [(k, self.held.pop(k)) for k in a.waiting if k in self.held]
            self.ready += [g for _, g in woken]

            def back():
                a.ref = a
                self.held.update(woken)
        if trail is not None:
            trail.append(back)
        return True

    def run(self):
        n = 0
        try:
            while n < len(self.ready):
                n += 1
                self.ready[n - 1]()
        finally:
            del self.ready[:n]
        return n

# CP-POSING: incremental
#
# PROVENANCE
#   author: implementation-python (an agent: Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5), 2026-11-27
#   seen a precursor (absys E01-E09): no
#   primary program of stdlib-concurrency for P07a, written before any program was run
#   idioms:
#     - the stage loop, cp calls: harnesses/python/README.md, sections 3 and 8
#     - one thread per held relation, waiting on a condition variable until
#       the information it needs has arrived: The Python Library Reference
#       (3.13), "threading -- Thread-based parallelism": "Thread Objects"
#       (daemon threads), "Condition Objects" (wait_for, notify_all, the
#       with statement on a condition); the same threads as this
#       configuration's P02 programs
#     - integer arithmetic, // and % on integers: The Python Language
#       Reference (3.13), "Binary arithmetic operations"
#     - assignment expressions, while and for statements, dict, list:
#       The Python Language Reference, "Assignment expressions", "The while
#       statement", "The for statement"
#
# P07a. One stage: x + y + z = <k>, y + z = <k>, z = <k>, in the instance's
# order (s.params["order"] names the relations by their position as
# written: 1, 2, 3). x + y + z = k is written decomposed (SPECIFICATION.md,
# "Arithmetic and comparison"), as x + y = t and t + z = k, with the fresh
# unknown t.
# All unknowns are integers. Python has no unknowns: each relation is
# held, as its places, until its evaluator (=, +, -, *) can compute a place
# or test it, and then decided. A place is the name of an unknown (a str) or
# an integer.
# Each relation, when it arrives, is given a thread of its own, which decides
# it by its evaluator once it can, and until then waits on the condition
# `changed`, which every new binding notifies. The main thread ends a stage
# when no relation thread is busy: each is waiting or done.

import threading

# CONSTANTS BEGIN
# stage 1
SUM_XYZ = 12
SUM_YZ = 7
Z_VALUE = 3
# CONSTANTS END

UNKNOWNS = ("x", "y", "z")

changed = threading.Condition()   # guards everything below; notified at every change
known = {}       # the bindings: unknown -> value
waiting = []     # relations whose threads wait for a value: (name, places)
failed = []      # relations found not to hold
count = {"busy": 0, "news": 0}    # relation threads not waiting; bindings made so far

cp.bindings(known)
cp.suspended("relations waiting in their threads", waiting)
cp.held("relations found not to hold", failed)


def equal(a, b):
    """The relation a = b. Each place is an integer, or None if unknown.
    Returns both places with every one that can be computed, False if the
    relation does not hold, or None if it must wait."""
    if a is not None and b is not None:
        return (a, b) if a == b else False
    if a is not None:
        return a, a
    if b is not None:
        return b, b
    return None


def plus(a, b, c):
    """The relation a + b = c over integers. Each place is an integer, or
    None if unknown. Returns the places with every one that can be
    computed, False if the relation does not hold, or None if it must wait."""
    if a is not None and b is not None:
        if c is None:
            return a, b, a + b
        return (a, b, c) if a + b == c else False
    if a is not None and c is not None:
        return a, c - a, c
    if b is not None and c is not None:
        return c - b, b, c
    return None


def minus(a, b, c):
    """The relation a - b = c over integers, as plus."""
    if a is not None and b is not None:
        if c is None:
            return a, b, a - b
        return (a, b, c) if a - b == c else False
    if a is not None and c is not None:
        return a, a - c, c
    if b is not None and c is not None:
        return b + c, b, c
    return None


def times(a, b, c):
    """The relation a * b = c over integers, as plus. Where the known
    factor is 0 and c = 0, the relation holds for every value of the other
    factor, which stays unknown (None); where c is not a multiple of the
    known factor, no integer satisfies it."""
    if a is not None and b is not None:
        if c is None:
            return a, b, a * b
        return (a, b, c) if a * b == c else False
    if a is not None and c is not None:
        if a != 0:
            return (a, c // a, c) if c % a == 0 else False
        return (a, None, c) if c == 0 else False
    if b is not None and c is not None:
        if b != 0:
            return (c // b, b, c) if c % b == 0 else False
        return (None, b, c) if c == 0 else False
    return None


cp.relations(equal=equal, plus=plus, minus=minus, times=times)

EVALUATOR = {"=": equal, "+": plus, "-": minus, "*": times}


def place(p):
    """The value of a place: an unknown's value, None while it has none."""
    return known.get(p) if isinstance(p, str) else p


def told():
    """With `changed` held, after a new binding: wake every waiting
    relation thread, counting it busy from now."""
    count["news"] += 1
    count["busy"] += len(waiting)
    waiting.clear()
    changed.notify_all()


def hold(rel):
    """The thread of one relation: decide it, waiting while it cannot."""
    name, places = rel
    with changed:
        while (outcome := EVALUATOR[name](*[place(p) for p in places])) is None:
            waiting.append(rel)
            count["busy"] -= 1
            changed.notify_all()
            seen = count["news"]
            changed.wait_for(lambda: count["news"] != seen)
        if outcome is False:
            failed.append(rel)
        else:
            new = False
            for p, x in zip(places, outcome):
                if isinstance(p, str) and x is not None and p not in known:
                    known[p] = x
                    new = True
            if new:
                told()
        count["busy"] -= 1
        changed.notify_all()


def pose(rel):
    """Give a relation that has arrived its own thread."""
    with changed:
        count["busy"] += 1
    threading.Thread(target=hold, args=(rel,), daemon=True).start()


def settle():
    """Wait until no relation thread is busy."""
    with changed:
        changed.wait_for(lambda: count["busy"] == 0)


def report():
    if failed:
        print("no solution: these relations do not hold:", failed)
    elif any(n in known for n in UNKNOWNS):
        cp.answer(", ".join("%s = %d" % (n, known[n]) for n in UNKNOWNS if n in known))


while (s := cp.stage()) is not None:
    if s.k == 1:
        relations = {
            "1": [("+", ("x", "y", "t")), ("+", ("t", "z", s.constants["SUM_XYZ"]))],
            "2": [("+", ("y", "z", s.constants["SUM_YZ"]))],
            "3": [("=", ("z", s.constants["Z_VALUE"]))],
        }
        for position in s.params["order"]:
            for rel in relations[position]:
                pose(rel)
    settle()
    if not s.replay:
        report()

# The Python harness

*Phase 4, wave 1, against `spec-1.0`. Written by the Python harness author
(`harness-python`, an agent) from the common contract in
[`../README.md`](../README.md), `systems/python/`, `PROTOCOL.md`,
`SPECIFICATION.md` and `METRICS.md`. Where the contract could not be
implemented as written, the reading taken is in
[`QUESTIONS.md`](QUESTIONS.md).*

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| [`run`](run) | the harness: `run CONFIGURATION PROBLEM SUBPROBLEM MODE PROGRAM OUTDIR` |
| [`runtime.py`](runtime.py) | the part of the harness that runs inside the program's interpreter process (the step meter, the `cp` calls, `observe()`) |
| [`check`](check) | `check CONFIGURATION PROGRAM`: compiles and reads the program's syntax tree, executes nothing |
| [`constants.py`](constants.py) | finds, checks and parses a program's constants block (used by `run` and `check`) |
| [`S-mechanisms.md`](S-mechanisms.md) | the S mechanisms each configuration provides |
| [`S/`](S) | extended's S mechanisms (`search.py`, `suspend.py`, `propagate.py`), with their tests in `S/tests/` |
| [`QUESTIONS.md`](QUESTIONS.md) | what could not be implemented as written, and the reading taken |
| [`qualification/`](qualification) | evidence that the harness does what this file says: [`qualify.py`](qualification/qualify.py) reruns all of it; [`output.txt`](qualification/output.txt) is its output |

Everything is written in **CPython 3.13.7 with its standard library**, as
the pinned `python:3.13.7` image provides it (`/usr/local/bin/python3`).
Nothing is installed. `run` and `check` are run inside the image, from the
repository root mounted at `/work`:

    container run --rm --platform linux/amd64 --volume "$PWD":/work --workdir /work \
        cp-agent-python:spec-1.0 harnesses/python/run core P01 P01a behaviour PROGRAM results/python/core/P01/raw

## 1. How a run works

`run` is the harness process. It reads `harnesses/stages.json`, checks the
program by reading its bytes, and starts the program in **its own
interpreter process**:

    /usr/local/bin/python3 -B -s -P harnesses/python/runtime.py FD_IN FD_OUT

with the environment cleared to `PATH`, `HOME` and **`PYTHONHASHSEED=0`**,
standard input `/dev/null`, and standard output and standard error going to
files that `run` reads at stage boundaries. `-B` writes no `.pyc` files,
`-s` ignores user site-packages, `-P` keeps the runtime's directory off
`sys.path`. No other interpreter flag is set; the recursion limit is
CPython's default, 1000 (QUESTIONS.md, Q1).

`runtime.py` compiles the program's text, as `run` sends it with the
constants block's lines emptied (it never reads the file), makes a fresh module `__main__` for it
(`__file__` the program's path, `sys.argv = [path]`, the program's directory
first on `sys.path`, as `python3 PROGRAM` would), puts the name **`cp`** in
its globals, switches on the step meter, and `exec`s it in the process's
main thread. `run` and the runtime talk over two pipes (marshal frames). The
runtime never runs program code of its own accord: the program runs from
its first line, and receives a stage only when it calls `cp.stage()`.

For stage k, `run` does, in this order:

1. **pose**: tells the runtime stage k (and, in a reposed run, first replays
   stages 1 … k−1 the same way, one at a time, each waiting for the program
   to finish it);
2. waits for **main's part of the stage to end**: the program calls
   `cp.stage()` again (asking for the next stage), or its module ends
   (normally, by `SystemExit`, or by an uncaught exception), or its budget
   runs out (its thread is paused), or it is quiescent (section 6);
3. **spawn**s each computation the stage spawns (`stages.json`), in the
   instance's `spawn_order`, and waits for each to end its part (section 5);
4. **answers**: the answers each computation reported through `cp.answer()`
   while stage k was posed, up to the query's cap;
5. **observe()**: the runtime reads the objects the program registered
   (section 3) and the mode's measurements;
6. **print()**: what the program wrote to standard output while stage k was
   posed (after any replay), verbatim.

The safety limit covers 1–6 for an incremental stage and the whole run of
1 … k (replay included) for a reposed one (common contract, Q13). After the
last stage `run` tells the program there are no more stages (`cp.stage()`
returns `None`), gives the process 5 s to exit, kills it otherwise
(recorded in the attempt's notes), validates the record with
`harnesses/validate.py`, and exits 0; an invalid record is kept as
`<run_id>.INVALID.json` and `run` exits 3. Usage errors (unknown
configuration, mode or instance, a missing program, a program without a
valid `CP-POSING` line) exit 2 with no record.

Environment variables `run` reads, all optional: `CP_IMAGE_DIGEST` (the
launcher passes the image digest; recorded in `system_build.image`, else
null), `CP_PURPOSE` (`primary`, the default, `variant` or `qualification`),
`CP_VARIANT` (the hidden variant's id), and `CP_STAGES` (a stages file other
than `harnesses/stages.json`, used only by the qualification's made-up
problems and recorded in the record's notes).

## 2. The configurations

From `systems/python/README.md`. All three have every mode (`PINS.md`).

| configuration | what a program may use | spawn() | posing |
|---|---|---|---|
| **core** | the language, its built-in functions and types, and `cp`; no imports. Any other standard-library module it imports is an external mechanism, to be listed | one after another (`side_by_side: false`) | incremental or reposed, as the program declares |
| **stdlib-concurrency** | core, plus `threading`, `queue` and `asyncio` | side by side (`side_by_side: true`) | as declared |
| **extended** | core, plus the S mechanisms listed in [`S-mechanisms.md`](S-mechanisms.md): the package `S` (`S.search`, `S.suspend`, `S.propagate`, in [`S/`](S)), and nothing else beyond core | one after another | as declared |

The configurations differ, in the harness, only in how `spawn()` runs
computations, and in what a program may import: `check` rejects
`threading`, `queue` and `asyncio` outside stdlib-concurrency, and `S`
outside extended. Whether extended includes stdlib-concurrency's
modules is QUESTIONS.md, Q2.

**Imports of S (extended only).** In extended, and only there, the runtime
puts a package object named `S` in `sys.modules` before the program starts,
whose path is `harnesses/python/S`; nothing else is added to `sys.path`, and
no module of `S` is run until the program imports it. A program writes
`from S.search import search`, `from S.suspend import Var, Queue, deref`,
`from S.propagate import Store`, and so on. Those modules are imported by
the interpreter's own import system, whose instructions are counted as the
program's, as for any import; the instructions of `S` code are counted as
the program's, as it runs in the program's computation. In core and
stdlib-concurrency there is no `S`: `check` reports an import of it as an
error, and `run` gives the program's `ModuleNotFoundError`. Any other
import in extended is classed as in core (an external mechanism, to be
listed). The S mechanisms' tokens are counted once per mechanism for the
configuration (`S-mechanisms.md`), not in each program.

**Posing.** `systems/python/README.md` ("The same computation") allows both
ways in every configuration: a program that reads each stage as it arrives
is one computation (**incremental**); otherwise stages 1 … k are rerun
(**reposed**). The harness never chooses: the program declares which, by
one comment line (section 3). The same program text works both ways, since
a reposed run gives it stages 1 … k in order through the same `cp.stage()`.

**After budget**, every configuration **can continue**: the computation's
thread is paused at exactly its budget and, at the next stage, released
with a new budget of 10⁶ (10⁸) instructions, in the same process
(`continued_after_budget: true`). It then carries on with what it was doing
and receives stage k+1 when it next calls `cp.stage()`. (In a reposed
program every stage is a new process anyway.) **After an error** or a
**final timeout**, stage k+1 is posed by reposing 1 … k+1 in a new process
(`after-error`, `after-timeout`), in every configuration.

## 3. The contract a program must meet

A program is **one file** of Python 3.13 source in UTF-8. It is run as a
script: from its first line to its last, in the process's main thread.

### 3.1 Required lines

1. **Posing**, exactly one line, anywhere (by convention the first):

        # CP-POSING: incremental

   or `# CP-POSING: reposed`. Without it, `run` refuses the program (exit 2).
2. **Provenance** (`PROTOCOL.md`, "Writing a program", rules 1, 2, 8), a
   comment block after the posing line, beginning `# PROVENANCE`, giving the
   author (person or agent), whether the author had seen a precursor (the
   absys experiments E01–E09), and the source of each idiom used (a manual,
   a paper, a published program).
3. **Constants**, if the sub-problem has any: **one marked constants
   block**, which the harness reads and **the program never executes**.
   It runs from a comment line containing `CONSTANTS BEGIN` to a comment
   line containing `CONSTANTS END`, and is divided by comment lines
   `# stage k` (k a stage number of the instance). Under each `# stage k`
   come the constants that **stage k first uses**, one assignment of a
   literal value (numbers, strings, `True`/`False`/`None`, and tuples,
   lists, dicts and sets of literals) to a plain name per statement:

        # CONSTANTS BEGIN
        # stage 2
        A_VALUE = 3
        # stage 3
        B_VALUE = 4
        # CONSTANTS END

   Nothing else goes inside, and no constant of any stage appears outside
   it. `run` parses the block (`constants.py`) and gives the program its
   text **with the block's lines emptied** (line numbers kept), so none of
   these assignments runs and no name in the block exists in the program.
   Stage k's constants reach the program **only when stage k is posed**, as
   the dict `s.constants` that `cp.stage()` returns with it (`{"A_VALUE":
   3}` at stage 2), and again with stage k whenever stage k is replayed. A
   constant a later stage needs again is kept by the program (it may store
   what it received); it is tagged once, with the first stage that uses it.
   The same name may appear under two stages, with each stage's own value.
   This makes no anticipation (`PROTOCOL.md`, "Writing a program", rule 5)
   structural: before stage k is posed, nothing of stage k's constants is
   anywhere in the program's process (the qualification scans its whole
   memory). The program file is never read by the program's process; a
   program may not read files (`open`, `__file__`, `linecache`, `inspect`,
   ...), which `check` rejects. The verifier replaces the block's lines and
   nothing else, so the program must stay correct for any other values of
   the same shapes. A program with no block is recorded
   `constants.how = "none"` (right only for P04d, P04f and P08b). Sizes n,
   orders and answer modes are not constants: they come from `cp` (below).
   A block that does not parse, an entry before any `# stage k` line, or a
   stage the instance does not have makes `run` refuse the program (exit 2).

### 3.2 The names `cp` gives the program

`cp` is a global the runtime puts into the program's module before its first
line runs. It is never imported. Everything below is a harness call (H).

| call | what it does |
|---|---|
| `cp.stage()` | **Receive the next stage.** Called only from the main thread. Returns a stage object `s`, or `None` when the harness has no more stages for this run (then the program should end). ### 3.4 Spawned computations (P09a, P09b, P16b)

After main's part of a spawning stage, the harness spawns each computation
in `stages.json` order (the instance's `spawn_order` for P09a), by calling
the function the program registered with `cp.computation()`, in a thread
the runtime starts in the same interpreter: one database (the program's

Each has its own budget, from its start, and its own execution state,

as spawned, with an undetermined state and a note. All three configurations
let spawned computations share unknowns (they share every object), so

### 3.5 What observe() reads, and the execution state

At the end of each stage (and, for a computation stopped by its budget, at
the moment it stopped), the runtime reads every registered object of every
computation of the stage and writes `observe.raw` as one line per object:

    main.bindings = {'a': 3}
    main.suspended[waiting relations] = ['s = a + b']
    A.pending[frontier] = [(1, 2), (2, 1)]

Each object is rendered exactly as `repr()` renders it, computed iteratively
for `list`, `tuple`, `dict`, `set` and `frozenset` (so deep nesting does not

a harness fault, recorded). `observe.bindings` is the bindings mapping split
by key (`A:x` for a spawned computation's), each value so rendered.
**Nothing unregistered is read**, and nothing is ever inferred from the
posed information: a residual the program holds but did not register is not
reported.

The execution state of each computation, as far as the harness can tell:

| state | when |
|---|---|
| `budget` | its thread was paused at exactly its budget |
| `timeout` | the safety limit stopped the process before it ended its part |
| `error` | an uncaught exception ended it (its traceback, as the interpreter prints it, is `error_verbatim`), or the interpreter process died (signal, exit status and stderr) |
| `alternatives pending` | its registered pending structures hold entries |
| `suspended` | its registered waiting structures hold entries, or it was quiescent (then `determined: false`: section 6) |
| `finished` | none of the above |

- **Step**: one CPython 3.13.7 bytecode instruction executed in Python code
  (`step_unit` in the record). Work inside built-ins is not counted.
- **Budget**: 10⁶ instructions per stage and computation (10⁸ for P12, P13,
  P16), from the start of the stage's window: the program's start for
  stage 1 or a new process, the posing of stage k otherwise, the release
  for a continued stage. A reposed stage's budget is its restart cost plus
  10⁶ (10⁸). When the next instruction would exceed it, the computation's
  thread waits inside the monitoring callback, so the count is exactly the
  budget and nothing in the program can catch or delay it. A loop inside
  one C call executes no instruction and is stopped only by the safety
  limit.
- **Restart cost**: measured in-run: main's instruction count at the moment
  stage k is first given to the program in a reposed run, after the replay
  (`restart_cost_method: "in-run"`). If the replay itself is stopped (by a
  replayed stage's budget, an error or the safety limit), stage k is never
  posed, and the restart cost is the replay's whole count (QUESTIONS.md, Q4).
- **Repeated work**: `null`; the systems file names only problem operations
  counted by the program, which `problem_operations` reports per stage.
- **Alternatives**: the registered pending structures' entries
  (`by_type` by name), never a peak (none is recorded by the harness);
  `held_as` is `unknown` (the classifiers decide from the program), or
  `none` when nothing is registered.

## 5. Stopping a system at the safety limit

The safety limit (60 s, rerun 600 s; 600 s fixed for P12, P13, P16) is
timed by `run`. When it runs out, `run` sends **SIGKILL** to the program's
interpreter process (`safety_limit.how_stopped`), keeps the answers it had
collected, and records `timeout` for every computation that had not ended
its part. The process is gone, so the rerun of stage k is a reposed run of
1 … k (stage 1: a fresh run) under the raised limit, and the next stage
after a final timeout is reposed (`after-timeout`).

## 6. Quiescence

A Python thread waiting on a lock, an event or a queue executes no
instruction, and would otherwise only end at the safety limit. The runtime's
watcher samples, every 0.1 s, the instruction counts of the computations
that are running their part of the stage; if **all** of them are alive and
none has executed an instruction over five consecutive samples (0.5 s), it
reports them quiescent, with each thread's innermost Python frame. The
harness then takes their part of the stage as ended and records them
`suspended`, `determined: false`, with that frame as the basis: the harness
cannot tell mechanically whether the thread waits for information or is
inside a C call that released the interpreter lock. A blocked computation
that later runs again is not resumed by the harness; it may be by the
program's other computations.

## 11. What a program must provide

A program author cannot run anything before the program is fixed (only
the system harness's `check`, which executes nothing). So each system
harness's README says exactly, per configuration, how a program meets
these requirements; the common part is:

1. **Stages as units the harness can pose.** The program handles stage k
   when, and only when, the harness poses it, in the way the
   configuration receives stages (incremental, or by replaying 1 … k).
   Code for stage k does not depend on any later stage.
2. **Replay.** In a reposed run the program carries out every stage
   1 … k in order, replacements and withdrawals included, and accepts a
   replayed commit stage as the information x = v, with v as the harness
   passes it (the verbatim answer of the commit stage).
3. **Instance parameters.** The program takes n, an arrival order, a
   spawn order or the answer mode from the harness, as `stages.json`
   names them, and holds everything else.
4. **Answers through the standard mechanism.** Answers reach the harness
   only through the configuration's standard mechanism for answers, in
   the form the system harness's README fixes (for Python and ALGOL 60,
   printed lines with the delimiters it defines).
5. **State for observe().** Whatever the system does not expose by
   itself (a Python program's named pending structure, its counters of
   problem operations), the program exposes in the form the system
   harness reads. Counters that only count are H (`METRICS.md`).
6. **Constants for the verifier** (`PROTOCOL.md`, "Writing a program",
   rule 6). Every constant of every stage is in **one** place the
   verifier can replace without touching anything else, and the program
   stays correct for other constants. Which place is fixed per system by
   its harness README, not here, with this default:

   | system | where the constants are |
   |---|---|
   | ALGOL 60 | **input**: read with the input procedures as integers in the problem's encoding (`systems/algol-60/README.md`, "Values"), from a constants file the harness passes; recorded as `constants.how = "input"` with its SHA-256 |
   | Absys, SWI-Prolog, Python | **one marked constants block** in the program, between a line containing `CONSTANTS BEGIN` and a line containing `CONSTANTS END`, each inside a comment of the language, holding nothing but the constants, or **input**, as the system harness decides and documents; recorded as `block` or `input` |

   A sub-problem with no constants (P04d, P04f, P08b; `variants/README.md`)
   records `none`. Sizes n and arrival orders are not constants (they are
   not varied) and come from the harness (point 3).
7. **Provenance** (`PROTOCOL.md`, "Writing a program", rules 1, 2, 8): its
   author, whether the author had seen a precursor, and the source of each
   idiom, in a comment the system harness README places.

**H tokens** (`METRICS.md`, class H) are the per-system harness's own
calls as they appear in a program: the calls that pose stages, request
answers and print, the emit stub's binding, and output adapters (rule
13). Each system harness's README lists them, construct by construct,
before any program is written. Code a program adds beyond them is
classed by the rules of `METRICS.md`, not as H.

The same fixed-vocabulary holding in stdlib-concurrency is R. The explicit rescan order in core and the locks, thread creation, wakeups, readiness accounting, and settling in stdlib-concurrency are C under rules 1, 2 and 10. The workers use the external "'`threading` mechanism; that module is available in this configuration and is not S.

By contrast, extended'"'s "'`Relation(name, evaluate, places)` accepts an arbitrary evaluator and argument tuple. Its constructor and callable controller implement a reusable goal adapter over relations, including generic wait/bind/failure handling. I classed that adapter, its class framing, and its failure store as S under rules 12 and 19. It is an additional mechanism supplied by the programs, not one listed at phase 4. It has 196 tokens in each text and is identical across the seven programs. The `__repr__` method is H under rule 13, since it only renders already-held relations. The listed suspension queue contributes its phase-4 published implementation count of 537 tokens, once for extended; no frozen batch token table for that module was invented. There is no call to search or the finite-domain propagator, and suspend.py does not import search. The optional trail convention does not itself constitute use of search. The two supporting implementations therefore total 733 tokens once for this configuration, with their use listed for each extended program. Repeated copies in the batch texts remain covered individually in the token spans.

Rule 19'"'s boundary is ambiguous here: a fixed arithmetic dispatcher can also be described as a reusable constraint store, since its unknown names and constraint lists are arbitrary. I chose the fixed problem-vocabulary/interface distinction above. The rule does not formally say how broad a relation vocabulary must be to be “general over relations.” A broader interpretation would move some of the core and threaded holding code to S and require reporting an extended configuration. This is a substantive classification sensitivity, not a claim that such reuse is absent. The generic evaluator parameter in extended's Relation makes its S classification much clearer.

The four evaluators are split identically in every configuration, even where a particular program never calls one of them. Their mathematical signatures, value computations in every direction, fully known relation tests, zero-factor cases, and integer divisibility checks are P under rule 19. Tests of which places are None, and the verdict "'`return None` that a relation must wait, are R. Mathematical zero and divisibility tests are not scheduling tests. The evaluator bodies do not become S merely because a generic controller calls them. No class was inferred from branch coverage in a particular run. The shared evaluator definitions contribute 271 P and 194 R tokens per text, including their layout.

Stage constants are P. The compound P07a relation is decomposed with fresh t, as SPECIFICATION permits, without an extra argument or algorithmic reformulation charge. P07a'"'s traversal of the supplied relation order transcribes the problem's prescribed conjunction order; it is P, with the fixed "'`s.params[...]` read H. Fixed `s.constants[...]` reads are H under the harness'"'s section 7, including when nested in a P declaration. Separating commas follow rule 20. INDENT and DEDENT tokens belong to the construct they open or close, so a closing DEDENT can appear in its own span after a differently classed body.

I treated the report routines and the unknown-name mappings used only for reporting as H output adapters (rule 13). Their tests choose how to print a failure or binding already computed; they do not derive an answer from an alternative computation. This is a narrower reading than treating every output-format decision as non-H. Neither these tests nor the residual printers are credited with solving a relation. The harness's general phrase “any code that decides which result is reported” could be read more broadly than METRICS rule 13's output-adapter exemption; the latter is the basis of this decision.

All seven subproblems are judged expressible with reformulation in each configuration: the relation expressions are encoded and their evaluators dispatch on partial knowledge, which introduces R. This is expressibility of the integer relation, not a claim that every conjunction is simplified or every finite solution enumerated. Extended's judgement includes its supporting mechanisms, explicitly counted separately; it is not a claim of native Python suspension. This exposes a further ambiguity in the expressibility table's phrase “or supporting code”: I interpret the judgement per configuration, including the declared mechanisms of extended and identifying its additional program-supplied adapter. Applying that phrase to S even when considering an extended configuration would instead label the S-assisted implementation “not expressible.”

The hardest outcome distinction was between an equivalent residual and a solved answer. For P07b, P07c, P07f, and P07g, the observations read objects that the program actually holds and can reconsider, not a printed copy of the input. Those objects denote exactly the valid outcomes, so they are complete despite the empty "'`answers` array. Their `identical_to_posed` flags are true at the level of mathematical information: tuple/object encoding and queue keys do not add constraints. All unknowns retain their full integer domains; none of these programs imposes a finite search domain.

P07b'"'s residual is reducible: adding its equations gives x=7 and then y=3. P07c's one sum relation is reduced, as SPECIFICATION explicitly requires; a parameterization using subtraction is not a solved form in that document's restricted term grammar. P07f's contradictory conjunction denotes the empty set but does not announce inconsistency, giving complete/residual/inconsistency undetected/suspended. P07g retains one relation with the same unknown in both factor positions. Factoring x²−9 proves equivalence to x=−3 or x=3. It is reducible because the two explicit solutions have no undecided relation. Neither solution is enumerated, and no two search alternatives are materialized; both remain implicit in the residual. The answer-completeness observations retain that distinction.

Residual size is measured by primitive relations and occurrences of unknowns, not printed bytes or queue entries. Input and residual sizes are respectively 2 relations/4 unknown occurrences for b, 1/2 for c, 2/4 for f, and 1/2 for g. Repeated x counts twice in g. P07a's input has four primitive relations and eight unknown occurrences after decomposition; d/e have three relations and five occurrences. A solved or explicit empty outcome has no applicable residual-size or identical-to-posed flag, so those fields are null.

P07a solves in every relation order by deciding single relations as their values become known; the auxiliary t=9 is observable in core and stdlib-concurrency but is not a requested answer. P07d similarly obtains w=7. P07e detects that 15 is not divisible by 2 and prints a no-solution report. Its unresolved w is not an alternative solution to that inconsistent conjunction. I classed the reported empty set as explicit, with simplification null. The no-solution line occurs in stdout/print rather than "'`cp.answer`; it is nevertheless an explicit inconsistency report under the problem'"'s observations and the specification's printed-report convention. The registered failure store corroborates it.

All 72 cost/storage comparisons preserve these classifications, the printed reports, bindings, residuals, and boundary work counts. "'`mode_differences` is therefore empty. Storage mode adds zero-valued process-wide coroutine/async-generator counters; that is extra measurement, not different suspended work. Allocation figures and step costs may differ without changing a classification. Null peaks, repeated-work figures, and other missing measurements are unavailable, not zero (AMENDMENTS 3.1). No never-reached-stage or failed-replay case arises in this P07 set. Each run has only one stage, so no earlier conclusion is withdrawn.

The totals below count every batch text'"'s frozen tokens exactly once. They do not add the separately published 537-token suspension implementation, and the S column includes seven textual copies of the 196-token local adapter. Mechanism-level accounting counts that adapter once per configuration, as described above.

| Configuration | P | C | R | S | H | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| core | 2,117 | 217 | 2,658 | 0 | 1,215 | 6,207 |
| extended | 2,295 | 240 | 1,358 | 1,372 | 1,456 | 6,721 |
| stdlib-concurrency | 2,128 | 1,656 | 2,436 | 0 | 1,215 | 7,435 |
| All texts | 6,540 | 2,113 | 6,452 | 1,372 | 3,886 | 20,363 |

All 36 behaviour stages are semantically complete: 24 are explicit and finished (18 P07a orders, three P07d solutions, three P07e empty outcomes); twelve are residual and suspended. Of those twelve, three are reduced (c), six reducible (b/g), and three inconsistency undetected (f). Boundary suspended-work counts are two for b/f, one for c/g, and zero otherwise. All boundary alternative counts are zero. There are no mode classification differences, harness faults, errors, budget stops, timeouts, or unreached stages.
